text: Spinoza earned his living grinding optical lenses while developing a comprehensive rationalist philosophy known as Spinozism (also Spinozaism) grounded in geometric-demonstrative method, most fully expounded in his posthumously published Ethics (1677), which posits substance monism—identifying God with Nature (Deus sive Natura) as the sole infinite substance possessing attributes like thought and extension, from which follows strict causal determinism rejecting free will in the ordinary sense.

His Tractatus Theologico-Politicus (1670), published anonymously, pioneered historical-critical biblical interpretation by treating Scripture as a human product to be understood through its historical context and authors' intentions rather than divine dictation, while arguing for freedom of thought and expression as essential to piety and state stability.

These works provoked widespread bans and accusations of atheism, despite Spinoza's explicit identification of God with substance, marking him as a controversial figure whose rejection of anthropomorphic theology and superstition challenged both Jewish orthodoxy and Cartesian dualism.

Spinoza's emphasis on reason as the path to human flourishing through knowledge of necessities, intellectual love of God, and ethical conatus (striving for perseverance in being) influenced Enlightenment thinkers, secular biblical scholarship, and later philosophy, though his pantheistic monism and deterministic worldview remain debated for their implications on religion, morality, and politics.

text: In historical and communal contexts, debates intensify around Spinoza's 1656 excommunication (cherem) by Amsterdam's Sephardic synagogue, with rabbinic authorities and scholars in 2024-2025 questioning its ongoing validity amid preparations for the 350th anniversary of his 1677 death; proponents of lifting the ban cite evolving Jewish inclusivity, while opponents invoke enduring theological divergences, such as Spinoza's rejection of revealed prophecy, highlighting persistent tensions between philosophical rationalism and orthodox belonging.

section: Legacy and Influence > Ongoing Scholarly Debates and Recent Reassessments
text: In 2021, Spinoza scholar Yitzhak Melamed was denied permission by Rabbi Joseph Serfaty of Amsterdam's Portuguese Synagogue to film a documentary inside the premises, with the rabbi citing the cherem's ongoing validity and declaring Melamed persona non grata, exemplifying continued communal enforcement amid scholarly calls for reassessment.
